label: Claude Sonnet 5.5
output:
**Title: The Coolroom Incident, For Jonno Who Keeps Asking**

Jonno,

Mate. You've messaged me four times about the coolroom and I've got a feeling you'll message a fifth, so here it is in full. Read it on the tube or wherever you people read things now. Mum, if you're reading this, you already heard the short version and yes, I'm fine.

Here's how it went. Monday night, the compressor in the coolroom carked it. Quietly, too. No bang, no alarm, nothing. It just stopped, like a dog that's decided it's done and lies down in the middle of the road.

I walk in at 6.40 on Cup Day morning and it feels wrong straight away. You know that smell. Not bad yet, just *thinking about it*. I look at the thermometer and it says 11 degrees. Eleven. That's not a coolroom, that's a nice spring day in Ballarat.

And what's on the books for lunch? 140 covers. Set menu. Three courses. On Cup Day, when every single person who's booked has already had a champagne in the car.

I rang Phil, obviously. Raff was away, so it was me running the show, and I wanted the owner to know what we were dealing with. Phil listened to the whole thing and then said, and I'm quoting, "just make it work mate."

Just make it work. Mate, that's not a plan, that's a fortune cookie.

So I rang Wally from Coldline, the fridge guy. Lovely bloke. Can't come till Wednesday. The part has to come from Sydney. Of course it does. Everything's from Sydney when you need it today.

So now it's about 7am and I've got a dead coolroom, a full day of prep, and a pile of product that's got maybe a few hours before it starts becoming a legal problem. Here's what we did, and you can picture it.

**Phase one: Tetris.** We emptied the coolroom into every cold thing we owned. Both undercounters, the bar fridge (yes, the one with the lemons and somebody's lunch in it), and anywhere else we could jam a tray. You've never seen dairy packed so tight. It was like a Japanese train in there.

**Phase two: Marta.** Marta from the cafe next door heard what was going on and offered us half her walk-in. Just offered. Didn't even make me ask. I almost cried, and I'm not a crier, so you can imagine what you'd have done. The price is croissant credit. I now owe her roughly three weeks of staff meal. I've done the maths and I will be making her lunch until Christmas. Worth every cent. Marta, if you're reading this, you're a legend and I'm not just saying that because of the debt.

**Phase three: the beef shin.** This is the bit you'd have lost your mind over. 30 kilos of beef shin that had to get from our kitchen to Marta's walk-in, and the only route is the laneway. It was raining. Naturally. So me and Benny loaded it onto a milk crate trolley, which is a thing we built out of what I can only describe as hope, and set off down the laneway like two blokes smuggling a body.

Halfway down, one of the wheels fell off.

Just fell off. Clean. Rolled away from us. I watched it go. Benny looked at me, I looked at Benny, and neither of us said a word because we both knew that if either of us started laughing we'd drop the lot. So we carried the back end of a crate trolley the rest of the way, in the rain, with 30 kilos of shin, in silence. I've never been so close to Benny in my life.

**Phase four: the esky.** Meanwhile Kev, our dishy, who I'd like it on record is the unsung hero of this entire story, took the old esky down to the servo and bought ice. He bought 14 bags. Fourteen. The guy on the counter looked at him and said, "Having a party?"

"Something like that," said Kev. And then he walked out with it like he was carrying a body to a lake. I love him.

Now. Service.

I'd love to tell you we had a smooth run, but you know me, I don't lie to you. Well, I do, but not about food.

By about 12.15 we had to 86 the panna cotta. It had been in a fridge that was at the wrong temperature at the wrong time, and it wasn't going to set the way it needed to. So the dessert course became "affogato with whatever." And I'm not exaggerating when I say people loved it more. More! I've been plating panna cotta for years, with a little compote, a little tuile, some careful nonsense, and the thing people wanted was ice cream and coffee with whatever we had lying around. I'm trying not to take it personally.

Then there's the lady on table 9. She'd been watching out the window, and she saw us. Two blokes and a one-wheeled trolley, in the rain, carrying meat down a laneway. When the beef came out she asked our waitress whether it was, and I swear to god this is true, "free range from the laneway."

It was. It was the freest range that beef ever had.

Here's the thing, though, and I'm going to say this once so don't make it weird. It was honestly the best service we did all year. Everyone was locked in. Nobody was whinging, nobody was drifting, nobody was on their phone. When a kitchen's got nothing to lose and everything on fire, people stop pretending and just *cook*. Benny was a machine. Kev was somehow in four places at once. The pass was quiet, tight, calm. 140 covers out the door, all good, nobody got sick, and I came out the other side feeling like we'd got away with something.

Total damage, in case you're wondering, was about 1800 bucks of stock. Mostly dairy, and the duck legs. RIP to the duck legs. They were good legs.

And because the universe clearly wasn't done with me, my horse in the sweep was called Ice Cold Lad. Ice Cold Lad. Came second last. I couldn't write that if I tried. The whole day was a bit and the horse was the punchline.

Wally came Wednesday and fixed it, by the way. Part from Sydney, as threatened. The coolroom hums again and it's the most beautiful sound I've ever heard. I stood in there for a bit on my own on Wednesday arvo, just breathing the cold air, like a lunatic.

Anyway. This is what I've learned, and I think it should go on a plaque somewhere: bistro kitchens run on bar fridges and spite. That's it. That's the whole industry. Anyone who tells you it's about technique or passion hasn't had to run a Cup Day lunch out of a servo esky.

And I know exactly what you'd have done, Jonno. You'd have taken one look at that thermometer, gone pale, and said something like "should we maybe call someone." London's made you soft. You used to be a grill man. You used to stare down a Saturday night with a dead flat-top and a smile. Now you're probably complaining about the quality of the bread, or whatever you do over there, and having feelings about your commute. You would've cried at the wheel. I'm not even joking. You'd have stood in the laneway holding the broken wheel like it was a dead pet.

I miss having you on grill, you flog. The new guy's fine but he doesn't talk shit at the right times, and he thinks it's normal to be quiet on a Friday night. It isn't. Someone needs to be telling a stupid story while the dockets are flying.

So that's the story, you can stop messaging me. Or don't, I like hearing from you. But read the blog next time instead of asking me to type it out. Forty people read this thing, and one of them is my mum, and she's already been told twice.

Come home, ya flog.

Aidan
